question: Sectoral operators claim that the recreational boating community as a whole is still very vulnerable to insurance fraud because the competent authorities, surveyors and insurers are not communicating in real time and because the transnational accident database needed to promptly cross-check accident data has yet to be created.

The recreational boating insurance market has been hit hard by fraudsters, whose go-to scams include bogus theft and shipwreck claims and ‘double-dipping’, a practice in which policy holders collect benefits from two or more insurance companies for the same loss or damage.

Given the cross-border nature of these scams, the Union could, by taking a proactive stance, make a key contribution to bolstering cooperation and data interoperability among the Member States. In the light of the above, could the Commission clarify: 1.

Whether the EU already has (or is in the process of setting up) any initiatives, programmes or databases designed to tackle insurance fraud in recreational boating, or whether it has made funding available to any projects akin to the above?
Whether it will establish a harmonised regulatory framework for the cross-border sharing of maritime accident information which also complies with the EU’s personal data protection legislation?
Which EU regulations could serve as a basis for the establishment of an interoperable and EU-wide maritime insurance fraud prevention system?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.10.2026) At present, the Commission is not pursuing initiatives, programmes or databases dedicated to tackling insurance fraud in recreational boating and is not aware of any EU-funded project specifically addressing this particular issue.

Investigating and sanctioning insurance fraud falls within the competence of the Member States, while the insurance industry can complement these efforts by developing fraud detection systems based on data sharing and analytical tools1 to identify potentially fraudulent claims and, where appropriate, refer them to the competent law enforcement authorities.

Directive 2009/18/EC2 establishes the European Marine Casualty Information Platform (EMCIP)3 a centralised database and data distribution system operated by the European Maritime Safety Agency designed to store, manage and analyse comprehensive data regarding marine casualties and incidents across the EU. EMCIP complies with the EU data protection legislation.

However, Directive 2009/18/EC explicitly excludes pleasure yachts and pleasure craft not engaged in trade from its scope unless the vessel is crewed and carries more than 12 passengers for commercial purposes or if the recreational craft is involved in a maritime casualty or incident with a commercial ship that is covered by the Directive.
Directive 2009/138/EC (‘Solvency II’)4 is a prudential and supervisory framework, and as such cannot serve as a basis for the establishment of an EU-wide maritime insurance fraud prevention system.

While the Directive provides for the exchange of confidential information between national supervisory authorities, these provisions cannot form the basis for an insurer-to-insurer claims or fraud-information exchange system.
1 To the extent allowed under the General Data Protection Regulation (OJ L 119, 4.5.2016, pp. 1–88) and

competition rules. 2 Directive 2009/18/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 April 2009 establishing the fundamental principles governing the investigation of accidents in the maritime transport sector and amending Council Directive 1999/35/EC and Directive 2002/59/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council, OJ L 131, 28.5.2009, pp. 114–1270. 3 https://emsa.europa.eu/emcip.html.
4 Directive 2009/138/EC on the taking-up and pursuit of the business of insurance and reinsurance, OJ L 335, 17.12.2009, pp. 1–155.
